metadata.note: The Denver & Rio Grande's Aspen Branch, built 1886-1887 down the Roaring Fork River valley from the D&RG's Tennessee Pass main line at Glenwood Springs to the booming silver town of Aspen, racing the rival Colorado Midland (which reached Aspen roughly three months later, in early 1888). The first train reached Aspen November 1 1887 over 3-foot narrow gauge track. drgw.net states the branch, like the rest of the route, was widened to standard gauge 'by late 1890' -- used here as the gauge-conversion date -- though other, less specific search-summary sources place that conversion as late as 1902-1906; this conflict is recorded rather than silently resolved (see not_yet_sourced). Aspen's silver boom collapsed after the Sherman Silver Purchase Act's repeal triggered the Panic of 1893 (the D&RG itself entered receivership Aug 2 1893); no source checked here gives Aspen-Branch-specific passenger timetable detail for the following decades of decline, so post-panic headway is a rough guess, flagged as such. COMPANY/COLOR SPLIT (CLAUDE.md Rule 4): the branch is split into two features at the Denver and Rio Grande Western Railroad's Aug 1 1921 formal takeover (the reorganization following the original D&RG Railway's bankruptcy) -- pre-1921 segments keep the Denver & Rio Grande Railway's own color (#8B5E3C, matching data/denver_early_railroads.geojson), post-1921 segments use the reserved D&RGW color (#B5451B) -- both features share identical geometry. Passenger service persisted into the D&RGW era at a much-reduced level; beginning in 1937 the railroad ran Pullman-equipped 'snow train' specials to bring skiers to the young Aspen resort, but per aspendailynews.com 'the D&RG passenger train made its last trip through the valley on Feb. 24, 1948' -- used here as the branch's passenger-service end date. Freight service continued for decades after (cut back to Woody Creek in 1968, later serving coal traffic out of Carbondale, with the last significant freight run in January 1991 and final rail salvage in 2006) but per CLAUDE.md Rule 1 that freight-only tail is not drawn -- the feature ends where passenger service ended, in 1948.

geometry_sources: OpenStreetMap (via Overpass API, https://overpass-api.de/api/interpreter): the corridor is real-traced almost entirely from the Rio Grande Trail, the rail-trail built on the historic D&RG/D&RGW right-of-way between Glenwood Springs and Aspen -- pulled as railway=abandoned/disused ways tagged name='Rio Grande Trail' (and 'Rio Grande Trail Soft Surface'), plus a directly-named railway=disused way tagged 'Aspen Branch' and several ways tagged 'Denver and Rio Grande Western Railroad'/'Denver and Rio Grande R.R.'. Colorado Midland Railway and Coal Basin Branch ways (a separate, competing railroad and an unrelated coal spur) were explicitly excluded. 95 matching ways were snapped to 5-decimal-degree nodes and routed with haversine-weighted Dijkstra from a node near Glenwood Springs to a node at Rio Grande Park, Aspen (site of the historic depot). A few small graph fragments (gaps of 3.6m-55.6m between OSM ways that clearly continue the same trail) were bridged directly; one small, distant fragment (~362m away, evidently an unrelated trail spur) was left unbridged and excluded from the route. The routed path is 66.30 km (41.20 mi) long, matching drgw.net's documented branch length of 'approximately 41.2 miles' almost exactly -- strong independent confirmation the trace follows the real corridor. No known realignment occurred between the narrow-gauge and standard-gauge eras, so the same traced geometry is used for all years drawn.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: Exact year of the narrow-to-standard-gauge conversion: drgw.net says 'by late 1890' (used here), but unclear secondary sources place it as late as 1902 or 1906 -- not resolved. Exact passenger headway/timetable for any era on this specific branch (all headway_min values here are rough, unsourced estimates for a mountain branch line). Whether the branch carried any named regular passenger train besides the 1937+ 'snow train' specials. The precise pace of the post-1893 service decline (only the panic's start date and its general economic severity are documented, not a service-frequency timeline).
